title: Building a Portfolio: Netlify, Docker & Modern Deployment
content:
# Building a Portfolio: Netlify, Docker & Modern Deployment

## Why This Stack?

Building a portfolio that showcases your work requires more than just a pretty website. You need:

- **Local development environment** that mirrors production
- **Easy deployment** without SSH or complex CI/CD
- **Fast iteration** on design and content
- **Scalability** as your portfolio grows

Netlify + Docker gives you all of this.

## Architecture

1. **Docker** for local dev and reproducible builds
2. **Netlify** for hosting and deployments
3. **GitHub** for version control and automation

## Getting Started

Create a Dockerfile:

```dockerfile
FROM node:22-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev"]
```

## Local Development

```bash
docker build -t portfolio .
docker run -p 3000:3000 portfolio
```

Visit `localhost:3000` to see your site.

## Deploy to Netlify

1. Push to GitHub
2. Connect repo to Netlify
3. Set build command: `npm run build`
4. Set publish directory: `out` or `dist`
5. Deploy

Netlify handles the rest — SSL, CDN, continuous deployment.

## Example: nitsuah.io

The portfolio at https://nitsuah.io uses this exact setup. See the live example.

author: Austin H.
title: Building a Small Project: Ollama + Neon + Next.js
content:
# Building a Small Project: Ollama + Neon + Next.js

## The Stack

- **Ollama** — Local LLM inference (no API keys)
- **Neon** — Serverless PostgreSQL
- **Next.js** — Full-stack React framework

## Why This Combo?

- **Ollama** runs locally → no OpenAI costs
- **Neon** free tier → PostgreSQL without ops
- **Next.js** API routes → backend without separate server

## Setup

### 1. Install Ollama

```bash
wget https://ollama.ai/download
./ollama serve
```

### 2. Pull a Model

```bash
ollama pull mistral  # or llama2, neural-chat
```

### 3. Create Neon Database

Sign up at neon.tech, create a project, grab the connection string.

### 4. Next.js API Route

```typescript
// pages/api/generate.ts
export default async function handler(req, res) {
  const { prompt } = req.body;
  
  const response = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'mistral', prompt }),
  });
  
  res.status(200).json(await response.json());
}
```

## Database with Neon

```typescript
import { Pool } from 'pg';

const pool = new Pool({ connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

export async function saveResult(prompt, result) {
  await pool.query(
    'INSERT INTO results (prompt, result) VALUES ($1, $2)',
    [prompt, result]
  );
}
```

## Example: vhsbox

See https://vhsbox.netlify.app for a live example of this pattern.

## Deployment

Deploy to Netlify Functions or Vercel. Ollama stays local; API routes call it.

This pattern ships fast without the ops overhead.

author: Austin H.
title: Building & Deploying a Chrome Extension with CI/CD
content:
# Building & Deploying a Chrome Extension with CI/CD

## The Challenge

Chrome extensions are great for automation, but:

- Manual updates are tedious
- Testing across versions is hard
- Deployment to the store requires manual steps
- Parsing and AI features add complexity

## The Solution: Full CI/CD

1. **Code** → push to GitHub
2. **Test** → run linting, unit tests, E2E in CI
3. **Build** → bundle extension
4. **Deploy** → push to Chrome Web Store automatically
5. **Monitor** → track updates and errors

## Project Structure

```
auto-apply-plugin/
├── src/
│   ├── content.ts      # Content script
│   ├── background.ts   # Service worker
│   └── popup.tsx       # UI
├── .github/workflows/
│   └── deploy.yml      # CI/CD pipeline
├── manifest.json
└── package.json
```

## GitHub Actions Workflow

```yaml
name: Build & Deploy
on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run test
      - run: npm run build
      - name: Upload to Chrome Web Store
        run: npm run deploy
        env:
          CHROME_EXTENSION_ID: ${{ secrets.CHROME_EXTENSION_ID }}
          CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN }}
```

## API & Parsing

```typescript
// background.ts
chrome.runtime.onMessage.addListener(async (msg) => {
  if (msg.action === 'parse') {
    const result = await fetch('/api/parse', {
      method: 'POST',
      body: JSON.stringify({ text: msg.text }),
    }).then(r => r.json());
    
    return result;
  }
});
```

## AI Integration

Use Ollama or OpenAI API for parsing:

```typescript
const response = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({
    model: 'mistral',
    prompt: `Extract job details from: ${jobPosting}`,
  }),
});
```

## Example: auto-apply-plugin

See the live extension at https://github.com/nitsuah/auto-apply-plugin — fully automated CI/CD with AI-powered parsing.

## Takeaway

Chrome extensions don't have to be manual anymore. Full CI/CD + API integration + AI = shipping fast.

excerpt: A practical migration guide from Next.js 14 and React 18 to Next.js 16 and React 19, including the key breaking changes and fixes.
author: Austin H.
title: Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19: A Complete Migration Guide
content:
# Upgrading to Next.js 16 and React 19: A Complete Migration Guide ## Overview Next.js 16 and React 19 bring significant improvements. This guide covers key changes, breaking updates, and migration steps. ## Breaking Changes ### 1. React 19 Server Components Server Components are now default. Client components need explicit marking: ```typescript 'use client'; export default function MyComponent() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ; } ``` ### 2. Next.js 16 App Router The `pages/` directory is deprecated. Use `app/` instead: ``` app/ ├── layout.tsx ├── page.tsx └── api/ └── route.ts ``` ### 3. Async Server Components Server components can now be async: ```typescript export default async function Page() { const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/data'); return
{data}
; } ``` ## Migration Steps ### Step 1: Update Dependencies ```bash npm install next@16 react@19 react-dom@19 ``` ### Step 2: Create `app/` Directory ```bash mkdir -p app touch app/layout.tsx app/page.tsx ``` ### Step 3: Convert Pages ```typescript // Before: pages/index.tsx export default function Home() { ... } // After: app/page.tsx export default function Page() { ... } ``` ### Step 4: Update API Routes ```typescript // Before: pages/api/users.ts export default function handler(req, res) { ... } // After: app/api/users/route.ts export async function GET(request: Request) { ... } ``` ## Common Issues ### Hydration Mismatch Server and client render differently. Use `useEffect` for client-only logic: ```typescript const [mounted, setMounted] = useState(false); useEffect(() => { setMounted(true); }, []); if (!mounted) return null; ``` ### Image Optimization Next 16 requires explicit dimensions: ```typescript ``` ### Font Loading Use the new Font API: ```typescript import { Inter } from 'next/font/google'; const inter = Inter({ subsets: ['latin'] }); ``` ## Performance Gains - **Turbopack** — Faster builds - **Tree-shaking** — Smaller bundles - **Image optimization** — Better performance - **Streaming** — Faster page loads with Suspense ## Deployment Deploy to Vercel or self-hosted: ```bash npm run build npm start ``` ## Timeline - **Phase 1**: Update deps and fix types (1-2 days) - **Phase 2**: Migrate pages to `app/` (1 week) - **Phase 3**: Fix hydration issues (3-5 days) - **Phase 4**: Optimize features (ongoing) ## Resources - [Next.js Upgrade Docs](https://nextjs.org/docs/upgrading) - [React 19 Release Notes](https://react.dev/blog/2024/12/05/react-19) - [App Router Guide](https://nextjs.org/docs/app) Take your time. Test thoroughly. The improvements are worth it.
